blocks.text: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms. While sharing electrons, each atom completes its valence shell and attains the nearest noble gas configuration. The bond formation between two Cl atoms is shown below (Fig. 3.2). A covalent bond may be non-polar or polar in character. The bond between two Cl atoms is purely covalent and non-polar. The electronegativity of the two atoms is exactly the same, due to which, the bonded atoms remain electrically neutral and there is no charge on either atom. The other such molecules are H₂, F₂, Br₂ and I₂. Examples of polar covalent bonds are H–Cl, H-Br, H₂O, etc.

blocks.alt: Shell diagrams. A chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) with its electrons as red crosses, a plus sign, and a second chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) with its electrons as green dots. A thick arrow leads to the two atoms with their outer shells overlapping; in the overlap sit one dot and one cross, the shared pair. Each atom is labelled (2, 8, 8).
